chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Kahili, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I said, 'I pass along the road and the water from the drain flows over me at times when I know that the people are performing wudu.' He said, 'There is no problem with it. Do not ask about it.'

I said, 'And the rainwater flows over me, and I see change in it and I see in it traces of filth. The drops fall on me and it splashes on me, and the house has wudu performed on its roof which drips onto our clothes.' He said, 'There is no problem with that. Do not wash it. Everything that is touched by rainwater has become pure.'

key_terms.التَّغَيُّرُ: Change or alteration in color, smell, or taste that may indicate impurity
key_terms.الْمِيزَابُ: A spout, drain, or gutter through which water flows from a roof or elevated surface
key_terms.بَأْسٌ: Harm, problem, or religious objection; 'lā ba's' (no ba's) is a standard juridical formula meaning 'no problem'
key_terms.طَهُرَ: To become ritually pure; the verb form of taharah (ritual purity)

ai.seo_question: Does rainwater purify impure things according to Imam al-Sadiq (AS)?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes a foundational principle of Islamic jurisprudence regarding ritual purity (tahara): rainwater is a powerful purifying agent. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) was asked about two scenarios — wudu water draining from a spout, and rainwater containing apparent signs of impurity falling on a person or their clothes. In both cases, the Imam gave the same ruling: there is no problem, no washing is required. The final maxim — 'Everything that is touched by rainwater has become pure' — became a well-established jurisprudential principle in Shia fiqh.
